scenes: An extension is something you add to Silo.
It adds rules, a computer, or both.
Its manifest lists them: the rules, the recipe of the computer, what wakes that computer, and the tools it may use.
What ships with Silo uses the same manifest as what people add.
First example: registry rules.
It adds one rule: allow crates.io on main.
Nothing in it is executed, so it has no computer.
Importing it changes nothing.
It shows the rule it adds.
Installing it switches the rule on.
Second example: disk watch.
Every minute it measures a folder of main.
That is something executed.
So the extension ships a computer.
Its manifest names the recipe, and installing the extension makes that computer.
Nothing of an extension is executed inside Silo.
You can always see that computer.
That computer asks Silo for what it needs, through tools.
It can use only the tools its manifest names, and installing the extension grants them.
A tool reads, shows or protects.
Disk watch reads the folder /work on main.
It shows a panel and an alert in the app.
Where a tool applies to computers, you choose which ones when you install.
Something wakes an extension.
Disk watch wakes on a time, and nothing waits for it.
Third example: request check.
It wakes when a network request of main waits at the boundary, and Silo asks it.
It answers one of three things: let it go on, deny it, or hold it.
Let it go on is not allow: the rules still decide.
If it does not answer in time, the wait ends as its manifest says.
You can always see what wakes an extension.
Request check denies and holds by itself, because its manifest names that tool and you installed it.
A tool that protects names the computer it applies to.
Granting it sets a precaution on that computer, which rests on the extension.
No tool an extension can use grants or destroys.
There is no tool to allow a request, to open a network, or to drop a computer.
Only the rules it adds can allow something, and importing shows them.
